state: {"record": {"id": "REC-5808", "title": "Cognitive behavioural therapy for health anxiety delivered by nurses in general hospitals: the HEAL-CBT randomised trial", "methods": "Design: two-arm, parallel, individually randomised trial in six general hospitals. Participants: adult outpatients attending medical clinics who scored above threshold on the Short Health Anxiety Inventory (SHAI) and met diagnostic criteria for health anxiety on a structured interview. Randomisation: an independent clinical trials unit generated the sequence by computer, stratified by hospital, and allocated participants through a web system after baseline assessment. Interventions: up to ten sessions of CBT adapted for health anxiety, delivered by general nurses trained in a five-day course and supervised fortnightly; control participants received standard care from their medical team. Outcome: the primary outcome was SHAI score at 12 months, self-completed by post. Secondary outcomes included generalised anxiety (GAD-7), depression (PHQ-9), and health service use from hospital records. Masking: participants and nurses knew the allocation; research assistants who collected secondary outcomes by telephone were masked. Analysis: intention to treat, with multiple imputation for missing primary outcome data under a missing-at-random assumption; sensitivity analyses varied this assumption.", "results": "444 participants were randomised (222 per arm). Primary outcome data at 12 months were available for 186 (84%) in the CBT arm and 194 (87%) in the control arm. The main reason for missing data was non-return of postal questionnaires; reasons were similar across arms. SHAI scores at 12 months were lower with CBT (adjusted mean difference -2.9, 95% CI -4.1 to -1.7). Sensitivity analyses gave similar results. The number of CBT sessions attended ranged from 0 to 10; 71% attended at least six. Health service use did not differ.", "registration": "Prospectively registered; primary outcome and time point match the registry. A statistical analysis plan was published before the database was locked.", "other_notes": "Four participants in the control arm received CBT privately during follow-up; they were analysed as randomised.", "discussion": "The authors acknowledge that the primary outcome was self-reported by participants who knew whether they had received therapy, and that expectation could have influenced responses. They point out that the secondary anxiety outcome collected by masked assessors showed a similar pattern, and that differences persisted at 12 months, long after the last session, which they consider less compatible with a simple expectation effect. They also note that the control arm did not receive an attention-matched activity, so non-specific effects of contact with a nurse cannot be separated from the specific effects of CBT."}}

Thanks so much,
Helen Ortiz
Lakeside Family Clinic"

{"supplier_questionnaire": "Responsible Sourcing Questionnaire - Tamsin Textiles Ltd (apparel supplier, tier 1)

Q1. Do you publish a modern slavery or forced labour statement?
A1. Yes, published annually on our website and signed by our managing director.

Q2. How do you audit your own factories?
A2. Our two garment factories are audited annually by an accredited third-party social compliance auditor. The latest audits found minor findings on fire exit signage, since closed.

Q3. How do you assess your own suppliers (tier 2, e.g. fabric mills and dye houses)?
A3. Tier 2 suppliers complete our self-assessment questionnaire every two years. We do not currently audit tier 2 sites.

Q4. Do workers pay any fees to obtain employment?
A4. We do not charge workers recruitment fees. Some of the labour agents we use for seasonal staff charge workers a registration fee; we are phasing these agents out over the next two seasons.

Q5. Do you hold workers' identity documents?
A5. No. Workers keep their own documents; lockers are provided.

Q6. What are your working-hours practices?
A6. Overtime is voluntary and capped in line with local law. During peak season some lines exceed the legal cap with the written consent of workers, and all overtime is paid at premium rates.

Q7. Do you have a grievance mechanism?
A7. Yes, an anonymous hotline in the three main languages spoken by our workers, run by an external provider.

Q8. Have you had to remediate any forced labour or child labour cases?
A8. No remediation has been required to date.

Q9. Do you subcontract production?
A9. Only embroidery, to two approved subcontractors listed in our supplier register.

Q10. How are wages paid?
A10. Monthly, by bank transfer, with itemised payslips. Seasonal staff recruited through agents are paid by the agent, who deducts accommodation where workers use agent-provided housing.

Q11. Do you provide worker accommodation?
A11. We do not operate dormitories. Some agent-recruited seasonal staff live in housing arranged by the agents; we have not inspected it.

Q12. Are your audit reports available to customers?
A12. Summary reports are available on request under NDA.

Q13. Do you audit or monitor your labour agents?
A13. Agents sign our code of conduct when appointed. We have not audited them; we rely on worker feedback through the hotline, which has received no complaints about agents this year.

Q14. Any other information?
A14. We are working towards an industry sustainability certification next year."}
